subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the TypeScript module structure using the SDK, setting up scale proportions for a baby dragon model with a coordinate system where Y is up and Z is forward, then starting to build the model with the builder API.

I'm working out the skeleton structure, placing the pelvis as the root joint and building a spine chain through catmull-spline points running from pelvis up through waist to chest, with the neck and head positioned forward and upward from there to give the sitting dragon a forward-leaning posture.

Continuing with joints for the jaw hinge and beginning the tail chain curving back and down from the pelvis, using catmull points to shape its sway.

Now I'm working out the hind leg joints for the sitting pose, placing hip, knee, and ankle positions to fold the legs forward naturally.

Now I'm planning the front legs as short arm chains from shoulder to elbow to wrist near the chest, tagged with an "arm" role, plus wing chains extending from the shoulders backward through elbow and wrist points to form partly-spread membrane wings since the dragon can't fully fly.

Adding wing fingers and membrane...

I'll use a surface raycast from above each spine point to find the body's top ridge, then plant a spike there angled backward along the spine rather than guessing at embedded positions.

For the body itself, I need to construct it first using a loft along the spine chain, defining width/height stations from waist to chest to get that egg-shaped belly profile.

Checking how loft handles bending: it builds its own catmull path through stations, but I can still attach a bone (the spine chain) so the body deforms correctly with the joints, passing it through sweep options.

For the color, I'm layering paints: countershading from teal back to a buttery belly tone, with a scales texture underneath so the body reads as dragon-like skin rather than flat color.

For the head, I'm attaching a rigid sphere part at the head joint, scaled unevenly to make it wider and longer for a snout-like shape, then adding a separate box part for the snout and small amber spheres with dark pupils for the eyes.

Still placing head features...

Working through the offset math confirms the sphere sinks about 0.017 into the surface as intended. Now I'm placing the pupil, seating it against the front of the eye using the same stick/hit approach.

I'll just place the pupil at an approximate center around z=0.30-0.31 with a small radius so it protrudes slightly in front of the eye surface, good enough without exact geometry. I still need to check whether that x,y position actually lands on the head sphere's surface.

Now I'm working out the jaw and mouth: placing a lower jaw box at the jaw joint in a buttery color, then adding small cone-shaped teeth along the upper and lower jaw for the grin effect.

Still placing jaw geometry...

For the cones pointing down for teeth, I'll orient them using a down direction vector so the tip faces downward, accepting it won't be perfectly verified visually. I also want to add a small smoke wisp from a nostril using a few shrinking, fading grey-white spheres.

Adding smoke sweep path...

Now moving to wing details — I'll set up a shoulder joint and a chain for the wing arm using a catmull path, parented to the chest.

Still working out finger bone rigging...

Working out the ruled membrane geometry...

Trying to simplify further, I'll just pick a membrane between the wing arm chain and a short polyline from wrist to finger tip, accepting some degeneracy in edge lengths since a full matching setup is overkill for the time I have.

Actually, a flat scalloped polygon for the whole wing membrane is simpler and more robust than chaining multiple membrane edges — I'll build the wing as a thin prism polygon through the shoulder, wrist, finger tips, and body side points instead.

I'm deciding to bind the wing membrane to the wrist bone since that's where it's anchored, keeping the rig simple even though the membrane spreads further out. For color I'll just keep it a solid amber rather than adding a gradient, simpler and still reads fine.

Now I'm working out the finger rods running from wrist to each tip, binding them to the wrist joint, and making sure each rod call includes an explicit color option since the sweep function requires one rather than inheriting it automatically.

I'm setting up the mirroring logic for left/right sides using a sign multiplier on the X coordinate, with joint names suffixed L or R, then defining the hind leg chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints parented to the waist and tagged with a "leg" role.

Still placing foot geometry and toes, then starting the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the chest.

For naming I'm renaming the arm joints to "armShoulderL", "elbowL", "pawL" to avoid clashing with the wing's wrist joint, and setting the wing chain as three points—shoulder, elbow, and tip ("wingL1", "wingL2", "wristL")—parented to the chest near the existing chest joint position.

Then I'm laying out the spine with three points (waist, chest) feeding the body loft bone, and working through the neck chain with three catmull points spanning into two named joints ("neck1", "neck2"), figuring out how the head joint attaches off the second neck point despite the slightly awkward positioning.

Next I'm building the tail: a four-point catmull chain parented to the waist with three named spans ("tail1", "tail2", "tail3"), then sweeping it with a tapering radius profile from thick at the base to thin at the tip, before planning a spade shape attached at the tail's end, oriented using the tail's direction and a face normal computed via Newell's method.

Defining spade polygon coordinates...

Still refining tail geometry...

I'm positioning the spade shape to sit flush with the tail's final joint, picking a dark teal tone for the fin color. For the spine ridges, I'm considering raising orange spikes along the back using a surface-and-ray projection approach from the lofted body geometry.

For each spine I'll shoot a ray down onto the body surface to find the hit point, then place a small cone-shaped spike there with a tilted direction, colored orange and sized around 0.035 length and 0.012 radius, spacing them along the z-axis to form a row down the back.

Now for the body shape itself, I'm lofting stations along the spine path to get an egg-like belly profile — wider through the midsection and narrowing toward the neck base — and building a matching bone chain for the spine so the mesh can deform naturally, with the loft colored using the countershading scheme.

For materials, I'm pairing a teal scale pattern on the back with a lighter belly tone, blending them based on surface normal height so the underside naturally lightens. The neck carries through as part of the same loft, while the head stays a separate joint with a sphere, using the same countershaded paint, and I'm adding a pair of small stubby horns placed on the head surface.

Now I'm working out horn placement and orientation using a downward raycast to find the head's surface point, then growing a tapered spike tilted backward with a cream color, weighted to the head joint. I'm also adding a lower jaw box piece positioned beneath the head, working out its exact vertical offset so it sits flush against the head's underside.

Still placing teeth cones...

Now for eyes, I'll make amber spheres with a small segment count, attaching them near the head surface using a nearest-point lookup.

Then I'm stacking a smaller dark pupil sphere onto the eye part's frame, embedding it slightly so it sits flush against the eye surface.

That math puts the pupil too close to center, basically hidden inside the eye given its radius. I should just position the pupil manually, offsetting it outward along the eye's axis by roughly 0.022 from the eye center instead of relying on the frame/embed calculation.

Checking the part/stick helper signatures — frame and "at" options derive weights properly from the parent part, so that should work fine for eyes. I'll skip the gleam detail for now and move to the smoke effect, which I'll build as a sweep along a catmull-rom path with its own color and radius function, noting the path itself has no bone owner so weighting falls back to nearest joint.

I'm calculating the nearest joint for the smoke path start point and defining a radius function that grows the wisp from thin to thick along its length — just a single sweep for simplicity rather than adding extra puffs, with default round caps.

Now I'm positioning the nostril on the head's front surface, working out the approximate coordinates using the head's ellipsoid radius and scale, then placing the smoke's starting point just above and in front of that nostril location. After this I want to add a speckled egg with a broken shell sitting nearby.

I'm working out how to build the broken shell using a lathe shape — the challenge is that a lathe profile needs a closed outline, so representing an open, jagged broken rim isn't straightforward. I'm considering constructing the shell as a bowl-like lathe where the profile runs from the base outward and up to the open rim, closing back along the axis.

Still working out the egg outline...

Closing the loop by tracing outer rim from bottom to top then back down along the inner rim, forming a closed crescent-like shape with thickness.

Still refining the rim zigzag coordinates...

I'm positioning the egg shell to the dragon's right side on the ground, lathe-centered with an upward axis, and planning a speckled paint pattern over a cream base using scattered teal spots to give it a broken, textured look.

Checking that points on the lathe axis (x=0) don't cause problems—those degenerate triangles should be harmless even where inner and outer bottom points coincide along the axis, and the closing segment between them should still work fine as long as the outline winding order is consistent.

Working out the egg shell proportions next—rim height around 0.12, bottom near -0.015, positioning the lathe so the bottom sits exactly at y=0. I'm also planning to add a small broken shard piece near the ground to sell the "broken shell" look beside the dragon.

Checking that nothing dips below ground level: verifying feet, tail, and hind leg positions all land at or above y=0, since the shard and feet geometry both need their lowest points resting right on the ground plane.

Right, legs are missing actual geometry—I need to sweep the thigh and shin chains with tapered radii, then do the same for the arm chains and wing-arm chains with their own thinner radii profiles, while the neck gets covered by a loft.

The neck needs an extra station since the current loft stops short of where the head actually sits, so I'm adding a station around y=0.39 with width/height 0.11, keeping the path at five stations total—weighting beyond the spine chain's last joint should just clamp fine. Now I'm checking that the body surface used for spikes lines up correctly with the loft sweep.

I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: spine as the root chain, then neck parented to chest, head parented to neck, jaw parented to head, tail parented to waist, and the limb chains (hip/knee/ankle for legs, parented to waist; arms and wings parented to chest) with left/right naming conventions. I'm also defining the head joint's position and aim direction, and starting on the jaw joint placement.

Working through the jaw's rotation math so it drops open naturally when posed — rotating about the X axis by a positive angle should pull the jaw tip downward to create a slight open-mouth grin pose.

Now checking that pose calls apply correctly after parts and bones are built, confirming teeth stay rigid with the jaw bone, and moving to the wing membrane slab which attaches to the wristL bone.

Writing wing point coordinates...

The projection should hold up fine despite the concave scallop shapes. For the right wing I'll just mirror the x-coordinates, then move to building finger rods from the wrist to each tip, setting up bone names and sweep paths for each one.

Since the wrist tip is actually a Joint object (which works as a Frame), I can reference the chain's tip property directly as the rod's starting point, with weights assigned per the bone rig rather than literal coordinates.

For the spines along the back, I'll cast rays downward at x=0 for a list of z-values to find the topmost surface, skipping any ray that misses geometry entirely—though I need to double check the head/neck sphere doesn't interfere with spine placement near the front.

Each spine is added as a small cone spike at the hit point, angled outward along [0,1,-0.4], tagged with a shared "spine" name, with five positions spread along the back ridge.

The paint operation on the head mesh preserves world-space positions through the chartify transform, so the sphere geometry stays correctly oriented with its UVs cut properly.

Writing the component code...

Setting up the color palette with teal scale tones, a deep shade, belly cream, and amber/orange accents, then applying countershading over the scale pattern to blend the hide colors naturally.

Building the skeleton chain now, defining spine and neck joints with Catmull-Rom splines through control points, double-checking that each chain's point arrays and parent joint references are typed and linked correctly.

Continuing with the head and jaw joints attached to the neck, then setting up the tail as a chain of points branching from the waist, verifying parent-child relationships stay consistent as I lay out each spline.

Checking that the station widths and bone chain line up correctly, and confirming the loft's radius function derives half-width and half-height from each station for the sweep.
